subsection: 5. Conflicts between economic interests and environmental interests

notes.h: Why conflicts arise
points: Economic interests: jobs, profit, energy supply, tax revenue, regional development and infrastructure.
Environmental interests: habitats, landscape, heritage, water and air quality, health, safety and the climate.
Interests conflict at local, national and global scales: a local community may oppose a project that the State or the world supports, or the reverse.

notes.h: Who is involved
points: Developers and companies, government and State agencies.
Local communities, which are often divided among themselves.
Environmental groups, farmers and fishermen, tourists, the EU and the courts.

notes.h: How conflicts are resolved
points: Planning permission, with appeals to An Coimisiún Pleanála (formerly An Bord Pleanála).
Environmental impact assessment, and court cases where decisions are challenged.
EU law, such as the Habitats and Birds Directives, which protect habitats and species.
Compensation, such as payments to turf cutters or to fishermen who give up fishing.
Compromise: route changes, limits on activity, conditions attached to permission and sustainable management.

notes.h: Corrib gas: the economic case
points: The Corrib gas field lies about 80 km off north-west Co. Mayo and was discovered in 1996.
Gas first flowed in December 2015 and was processed at the Bellanaboy terminal; for a time it supplied over half of Ireland's gas.
Economic arguments: energy security, a domestic gas supply, revenue for the State and the companies, and construction jobs.

notes.h: Corrib gas: local and environmental objections
points: The original plan piped high-pressure, unprocessed gas onshore near homes at Rossport, creating a safety risk for residents.
The Shell to Sea campaign, from 2005, argued that the gas should be processed at sea rather than onshore.
Sruwaddacon Bay, a protected estuary (Special Area of Conservation), lay on the route of the pipeline.

notes.h: Corrib gas: protests, changes and outcome
points: The Rossport Five were jailed in June 2005 for refusing to obey a court order not to obstruct pipeline work; they were released after 94 days.
Protests were policed heavily for years, and the dispute divided the local community.
The onshore route was changed to keep the pipeline further from houses, and a tunnel was bored under Sruwaddacon Bay to carry it.
Shell sold its share in the project in 2018.

notes.h: Irish fish stocks: fishing communities and EU quotas
points: Killybegs, Co. Donegal, is Ireland's largest fishing port; the six State Fishery Harbour Centres are Killybegs, Castletownbere, Dingle, Rossaveel, Dunmore East and Howth.
Under the Common Fisheries Policy (1983), total allowable catches are set by the EU and divided into national quotas.
Irish fishermen have long argued that Ireland's share of the catch in its own rich waters is too small, and much of that catch is taken by other EU fleets.
Ireland's exclusive economic zone extends 200 nautical miles from the coast.

notes.h: Irish fish stocks: Brexit and decommissioning
points: The EU–UK Brexit trade agreement (December 2020) reduced Irish quotas.
A scheme paid vessel owners to decommission (scrap) their boats.

notes.h: Irish fish stocks: the wild salmon drift-net ban
points: Ireland banned drift-net fishing for wild salmon at sea from 2007, because wild salmon returning to Irish rivers had fallen sharply.
Commercial salmon fishermen received compensation.
Anglers and conservation groups supported the ban, because wild salmon sustain angling tourism.

notes.h: Irish fish stocks: mackerel dispute and fish farming
points: From 2010 Iceland and the Faroe Islands set large mackerel quotas as mackerel moved north-west into their waters.

The EU, with strong support from Irish fishermen, protested; in 2013 it imposed trade measures on the Faroe Islands over its herring catches, banning imports of Faroese herring and mackerel; the dispute eased in 2014.
Salmon farms in western bays: anglers blame sea lice from the farms for harming wild salmon and sea trout.

notes.h: Mullaghmore, the Burren: the proposed visitor centre
points: The Burren, Co. Clare, has Carboniferous limestone pavement, with rare Arctic-alpine and Mediterranean plants growing side by side, such as spring gentian and mountain avens.
Mullaghmore is a hill of folded, terraced limestone; the Burren National Park protects the area near it.
In the early 1990s the Office of Public Works (OPW) began building an interpretative centre and car park near Mullaghmore.

notes.h: Mullaghmore: the two sides
points: Supporters: tourism jobs and visitor spending in a poor rural area, and better visitor management.
The Burren Action Group: traffic, sewage and visitor pressure would damage a fragile, unspoilt landscape, and any centre should be in nearby villages.

notes.h: Mullaghmore: legal challenge and outcome
points: In 1993 the Supreme Court ruled that the State had to obtain planning permission like any other developer, and work stopped.
In 2000 An Bord Pleanála refused permission, and the partly built site was cleared and restored.

notes.h: Skellig Michael: heritage and its setting
points: Skellig Michael, about 12 km off the Iveragh Peninsula, Co. Kerry, has an early Christian monastery of stone beehive huts on a steep rocky island.
It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996 and is managed by the OPW.
Seabirds, including puffins, Manx shearwaters and storm petrels, breed on the island; Little Skellig holds one of the world's largest gannet colonies.

notes.h: Skellig Michael: tourism pressures and management
points: Filming for the Star Wars films (from 2014) greatly increased demand for visits.
Boat operators and local businesses want more access; conservationists object to the filming and to rising visitor numbers.
Access is only by licensed boats in summer, with visitor numbers capped at about 180 a day; landings depend on the weather.
Steep steps and the weather make landing a safety issue.

notes.h: Hill of Tara: heritage
points: The Hill of Tara, Co. Meath, is an ancient ceremonial site and the traditional seat of the High Kings of Ireland.
The Tara–Skryne valley around the hill is an archaeological landscape; excavation along the planned road route found dozens of sites.

notes.h: M3 motorway: the economic case
points: The M3 runs from Clonee to north of Kells, relieving congestion on the N3 for the fast-growing commuter towns of Meath, such as Navan and Kells.
It cuts journey times to Dublin.
The route passes through the Tara–Skryne valley, about 2 km from the Hill of Tara.

notes.h: M3 and the Hill of Tara: objections and outcome
points: Campaign groups, archaeologists and protesters camped on the route argued that the road would destroy an archaeological landscape.
In 2007 a large prehistoric ceremonial enclosure was found at Lismullin and declared a national monument; it was excavated and recorded, and then the road was built over it.
The M3 opened in 2010.

notes.h: Turf cutting on protected raised bogs: the conflict
points: Turf cutting gives rural families a traditional right and a cheap source of fuel.
Raised bogs are rare in Europe and store large amounts of carbon; Ireland holds a large share of the EU's remaining active raised bog.
The EU Habitats Directive (1992) required Ireland to designate raised bogs as Special Areas of Conservation (SACs).

notes.h: Turf cutting on protected raised bogs: ban, compensation and protest
points: After a ten-year derogation ended, turf cutting was banned on 53 raised-bog SACs from 2011.
Compensation: about €1,500 a year for 15 years per turf cutter, or relocation to a bog that is not protected.
The Turf Cutters and Contractors Association organised protests, and some cutting continued on some bogs.

notes.h: Wind farms: renewables against local interests
points: Economic and renewable case: renewable energy targets, income for landowners and community funds.
Local objections: visual impact, noise, shadow flicker, falling property values, effects on birds, and peat stability.
Derrybrien, Slieve Aughty Mountains, Co. Galway: a peat slide of about 450,000 m³ on 16 October 2003, during wind-farm construction, killed fish in the Owendalulleegh River.
In 2019 the EU Court of Justice fined Ireland €5 million plus €15,000 a day because no proper environmental impact assessment had been carried out.
Offshore wind: the Climate Action Plan sets at least 5 GW of offshore wind, which can conflict with fishing grounds and seascapes.

notes.h: Dairy expansion, water and climate
points: Milk quotas were abolished on 1 April 2015, and the dairy herd grew strongly afterwards.
Economic case: farm incomes and food exports.
Environmental case: nitrates reaching water damage water quality; agriculture produces over a third of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions.
EPA (2016–2021): only about half of Irish rivers, lakes and estuaries were in good or high ecological status, with agriculture the main pressure.
Sectoral ceilings (2022) require agriculture to cut emissions by 25% by 2030.

notes.h: Data centres and electricity
points: Economic case: investment, multinational jobs and Ireland's technology economy.
Data centres used about a fifth of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO), and most are in the Dublin region.
Environmental and grid case: huge electricity demand strains the grid and works against climate targets.
In 2022 EirGrid said it would not connect new data centres in the Dublin area until about 2028, because the grid could not supply them.

notes.h: Amazon rainforest: economic drivers
points: The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest, with about 60% of it in Brazil.
Cattle ranching is the main driver of clearing, and most cleared land becomes pasture; soya farming spreads in the south.
Logging removes timber from the forest.
The Trans-Amazonian Highway, begun in 1970, opened the forest to settlers; clearings along the roads form a fishbone pattern, as in Rondônia.
Carajás, Pará, has the world's largest iron-ore mine, run by Vale.
The Belo Monte dam on the Xingu River, completed in 2019, was opposed by indigenous groups including the Kayapó.

notes.h: Amazon rainforest: environmental and global interests
points: The forest holds biodiversity, stores large amounts of carbon, recycles rainfall and is home to indigenous peoples.
Global interest: clearing the forest releases carbon that adds to climate change, while Brazil's development needs drive clearing.

notes.h: Amazon rainforest: deforestation trend
points: Satellite monitoring by PRODES: about 27,800 km² of the Brazilian Amazon was cleared in 2004.
Clearing was cut by over 80%, to about 4,600 km², by 2012.
Clearing rose again to about 13,000 km² in 2021.

notes.h: Amazon rainforest: protection measures and policy swings
points: Brazil's Forest Code requires landowners in the Amazon to keep 80% of their land as forest, though this is often not enforced.
The soy moratorium of 2006: major traders agreed not to buy soya from newly cleared Amazon land.
The Amazon Fund of 2008: donors, mainly Norway and also Germany, pay for reduced deforestation.
Deforestation rose under President Bolsonaro (2019–2022) and fell under President Lula (2003–2010, and again from 2023).

notes.h: Amazon rainforest: people in conflict
points: Chico Mendes, a rubber tapper and union leader who campaigned to protect the forest, was murdered at Xapuri, Acre, on 22 December 1988.
His murder shows that the conflict over clearing was one between people, not only between economic and environmental interests.

notes.h: Lignite mining in Germany: the Hambach Forest
points: RWE's Hambach open-cast lignite mine in North Rhine-Westphalia expands into the ancient Hambach Forest.
Economic side: the mine supplies power and jobs in the Rhineland. Environmental side: the forest, the villages and the carbon released by burning lignite.
Protesters occupied tree houses in the forest for years; in October 2018 a German court halted the clearing.
The remaining forest was later spared under the coal phase-out.

notes.h: Lignite mining in Germany: Lützerath and the coal phase-out
points: The village of Lützerath was cleared of protesters in January 2023 to extend the Garzweiler lignite mine.
Germany's 2020 law ends coal-fired power by 2038 at the latest.

notes.h: Three Gorges Dam, China: benefits
points: The Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River is the world's largest power station by installed capacity.
It provides clean electricity, flood control downstream and improved navigation.
The dam was completed in 2006 and became fully operational in 2012.

notes.h: Three Gorges Dam, China: costs
points: Over one million people were relocated.
Farmland, towns and archaeological sites were flooded by the reservoir.
The dam traps sediment that would otherwise reach the river downstream, and the ecology of the river has changed.

notes.h: Global versus local interests in climate policy
points: Developing countries argue for their right to develop with cheap energy, while the global need is to cut emissions.
Fossil-fuel exporting countries protect their revenue from coal, oil and gas.
Belém, Pará, hosted the COP30 climate conference in November 2025.

notes.h: Map-based question: locating a development
points: Identify the development and the features of the site it needs, such as a wind farm on high ground with open views, or a quarry close to a village.
Read the map for relevant features: contour lines for height, settlements, roads for access, rivers, and protected areas.
Identify the groups for and against: developers and landowners usually support a site, while residents, environmental groups and tourism businesses may object.
Conflict arises when a site serves one group's interests while threatening another group's interests; give the reasons for each side.

keyTerms.definition: A person or group with an interest in a development, such as a company, a community, a government agency or an environmental group.
A site protected under EU law for its habitats or species, such as the raised bogs and estuaries designated in Ireland.
A bog that rises above the surrounding land and stores large amounts of carbon, and is rare in Europe.
An exemption from a law for a set period, such as the ten-year period that allowed turf cutting on protected raised bogs.
A net left hanging in the water to catch fish, banned in Ireland for wild salmon at sea from 2007.
A soft brown coal, mined in open-cast pits in Germany's Rhineland and burned to generate electricity.
Parasites from salmon farms that are blamed by anglers for harming wild salmon and sea trout.
A visitor building that explains a site's natural or historic features, such as the one planned near Mullaghmore.

questions.prompt: Discuss how conflict may develop between economic interests and environmental interests, with reference to two examples that you have studied.
questions.model: Corrib gas, Co. Mayo: the economic case was a domestic gas supply from the field about 80 km off north-west Co. Mayo, which for a time supplied over half of Ireland's gas, with revenue and construction jobs. The local and environmental case objected to piping high-pressure, unprocessed gas onshore near homes at Rossport, and to the risk to Sruwaddacon Bay, a protected estuary. The Shell to Sea campaign from 2005 argued the gas should be processed at sea. The Rossport Five were jailed in June 2005 for defying a court order and were released after 94 days, and protests were heavily policed for years, dividing the community. The onshore route was changed and a tunnel was bored under Sruwaddacon Bay; gas first flowed in December 2015, and Shell sold its share in 2018. Irish fish stocks: fishing communities at ports such as Killybegs depend on quotas set under the Common Fisheries Policy, and Irish fishermen argue Ireland's share of its own rich waters is too small. Brexit reduced Irish quotas and led to vessel decommissioning. Conservation measures, such as the 2007 ban on wild salmon drift-netting, cost commercial fishermen compensation, while anglers and conservationists supported it. The mackerel and herring disputes with Iceland and the Faroe Islands led to EU trade measures against the Faroes in 2013, and sea lice from salmon farms harm wild salmon and sea trout.

questions.prompt: Examine one global example of conflict between economic development and environmental interests.
questions.model: The Amazon rainforest, Brazil. Economic drivers include cattle ranching, which is the main cause of clearing, soya farming in the south, logging, the Carajás iron-ore mine run by Vale, the Belo Monte dam on the Xingu River completed in 2019, and the Trans-Amazonian Highway begun in 1970, which opened the forest to settlers and created the fishbone pattern of clearings seen in Rondônia. Environmental interests include biodiversity, the carbon the forest stores, rainfall recycling and the land of indigenous peoples such as the Kayapó, who opposed Belo Monte. Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon, measured by PRODES, was about 27,800 km² in 2004, was cut by over 80% to about 4,600 km² by 2012, and rose again to about 13,000 km² in 2021. Protection measures include Brazil's Forest Code requiring 80% forest on Amazon landholdings, though often not enforced, the soy moratorium of 2006, the Amazon Fund of 2008 paid for mainly by Norway and also Germany, and indigenous reserves. Policy has swung with the government: clearing rose under President Bolsonaro (2019–2022) and fell under President Lula. Chico Mendes, a rubber tapper and union leader who campaigned to protect the forest, was murdered at Xapuri, Acre, on 22 December 1988, showing how the conflict was fought between people.

questions.prompt: (i) Name one example of how the development of economic activities has resulted in conflict between people. (ii) Describe and explain this conflict.
questions.model: Mullaghmore, the Burren, Co. Clare: the Office of Public Works began building an interpretative centre and car park near Mullaghmore in the early 1990s. Supporters argued that tourism would bring jobs and spending to a poor rural area and allow better visitor management. The Burren Action Group argued that traffic, sewage and visitor pressure would damage the fragile limestone landscape with its rare Arctic-alpine and Mediterranean plants, and that any centre should be in nearby villages. The conflict between people became a legal one: in 1993 the Supreme Court ruled that the State needed planning permission like any other developer, and work stopped. In 2000 An Bord Pleanála refused permission, and the partly built site was cleared and restored.
